newsitem.title: JAPAN: Okinawa anniversary to be marked by protests.
newsitem.headline: Okinawa anniversary to be marked by protests.

text.p: U.S. military bases on Okinawa tightened security on Wednesday ahead of expected anti-base rallies to mark the 25th anniversary of the restoration of Japanese sovereignty over the strategic, subtropical island.

Residents around the bases said some entrances had been closed and both Japanese police and U.S. military vehicles had taken up positions near the bases in what they said appeared to be a deliberate strategy to warn off protestors.
"Security around the bases is much tighter than normal," one longtime resident said.

Thursday's anniversary of Okinawa's 1972 reversion to Japanese rule after 27 years under U.S. administration was expected to be dominated by protests by citizens' groups and labour unions against the U.S. military presence.
The central and Okinawan governments, since 1995 at odds over how to deal with the island's heavy concentration of U.S. bases, were not planning any commemorative events.

The central government was expected to be a target of Okinawan protesters who accuse Tokyo of neglecting the complaints of Okinawa, Japan's poorest prefecture and host to about half of the 47,000 U.S. military personnel stationed in Japan.
The anniversary falls one day after central government leases on land for 12 U.S. military facilities on Okinawa expired but were forcibly renewed over the opposition of 3,000 anti-base landowners.

In a move that prompted skirmishes in parliament and the arrests of Okinawan activists, Japan's legislature last month voted to revise land laws to enable the government to continue providing the land for use by U.S. forces.
The anti-base landowners who were forced to renew leases on their plots at the huge U.S. Air Force Kadena Air Base were planning to press for permission to enter their land, activists said.

Other anti-base groups will rally at Futenma Junior High School, which lies next to a helicopter base and is seen by Okinawan activists as a symbol of the dangers and noise that come with living close to U.S. bases, they said.

Anti-base sentiment on Okinawa, scene of the last and bloodiest Pacific theatre battle of World War Two, festered for decades before exploding into island-wide protests after the September 1995 gang rape of a local schoolgirl by three U.S. servicemen.
Okinawa Governor Masahide Ota seized on the rape, for which the servicemen received lengthy prison sentences, to press for the complete withdrawal of U.S. troops from the island.

On Monday, a poll published by the liberal daily newspaper Asahi Shimbun to mark the 25th anniversary of the handover showed a 72 percent majority wanted the gradual removal of U.S. bases from the island.

But the April 20-21 random survey of 2,251 people also found that 76 percent of respondents nationwide -- but only 57 percent of Okinawans -- favoured maintaining the U.S.-Japan Security Treaty under which the United States maintains bases in Japan.
